output.query: warfarin cessation migraine aphasic aura TIA misdiagnosis anticoagulation overtreatment

results.summary: Studies show 30-50% of TIA diagnoses are incorrect; most common mimics are migraine with aura and functional neurological disorders; misdiagnosis leads to unnecessary anticoagulation and bleeding risk.
results.title: Reassessing chronic anticoagulation when the original indication is uncertain

results.summary: Long-term warfarin in patients without confirmed AF or documented cerebral infarction carries annual major bleeding risk ~2-3%/year, substantially higher with supratherapeutic INR.
results.title: Bleeding risk and benefit-harm balance of long-term warfarin therapy

results.summary: When a presumed TIA is refuted by imaging and a non-vascular alternative is identified, anticoagulation can be safely discontinued after definitive AF exclusion.
results.title: Approach to anticoagulation in patients with transient neurological events of uncertain aetiology

output.query: migraine preventive therapy postmenopausal woman after warfarin bleeding complication

results.summary: Amitriptyline and topiramate are first-line preventive agents; anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies well-tolerated in postmenopausal women; hormone therapy interactions minimised after natural menopause.
results.title: Migraine Prevention in Postmenopausal Women

results.summary: Four disabling migraine attacks per year or more = standard indication for preventive therapy; topiramate 25-100 mg/day or amitriptyline 10-25 mg QHS are recommended first-line options.
results.title: Preventive Therapy Indication in Recurrent Disabling Migraine

results.summary: In patients with migraine who are not receiving anticoagulation, NSAIDs and triptans are established acute treatment options; aspirin 900 mg has both acute and mild preventive benefit; combined OCP is contraindicated in migraine with aura regardless of anticoagulant status.
results.title: Acute Migraine Treatment and Anticoagulation

output.summary: Topiramate (25-100 mg/day, Level A) and amitriptyline (10-25 mg QHS, Level B) are recommended first-line preventive options for recurrent disabling migraine in postmenopausal women; anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies are well-tolerated in this population. NSAIDs and triptans are the established acute treatment options for migraine in patients not receiving anticoagulation.

output.query: aphasic migraine aura gradual onset cortical spreading depression TIA differentiation

results.summary: Aphasia developing gradually over 5-10 minutes is characteristic of CSD propagation in migraine; TIA aphasia is maximal at onset and does not characteristically progress gradually; this distinction has ~85% sensitivity for migraine when combined with subsequent headache.
results.title: Gradual vs Abrupt Onset in Transient Aphasia: Migraine vs TIA

results.summary: Severe migrainous headache following each transient aphasic episode is highly characteristic of migraine with aura; TIA does not predictably cause ipsilateral migrainous headache; this temporal pattern has high diagnostic specificity for migraine.
results.title: Subsequent Migrainous Headache After Transient Aphasia

results.summary: A first-degree relative with migraine with aura is associated with familial migraine predisposition; prior brief visual phenomena preceding aphasic episodes may represent earlier visual aura in a migraine-predisposed individual. Such features are supportive but are not in themselves diagnostic; clinical correlation required.
results.title: Family History and Prior Visual Aura in Migraine Predisposition

patient.history_present_illness:
A 46-year-old Australian woman presented to the neurology clinic requesting a second opinion after being started on warfarin 8 months ago for a presumed TIA. She has had four episodes over the past year of transient expressive word-finding difficulty lasting 15-25 minutes, each followed by a severe left temporal throbbing headache with nausea and photophobia lasting 8-12 hours. The treating team at a regional hospital determined that these were 'probable TIA events' and started warfarin after a work-up which included an MRI showing 'white matter changes' and an ECG reportedly showing 'intermittent AF.'

She is now bleeding from her gums and had a prolonged nosebleed last month. Her INR was 3.8 at last check (above therapeutic range). She has no personal history of stroke, no cardiac disease, and was entirely healthy prior to these episodes. On careful history review, she has had occasional brief 'light shows' in her peripheral vision for several years before the main episodes — these were 'like stars or sparkles' lasting 5-10 minutes and dismissed as tiredness.

On review of external records: the 'ECG showing AF' appears to have been a rhythm strip taken during a palpitation episode; she subsequently had a normal 24-hour Holter. The 'white matter changes' on the prior MRI report are described as 'small non-specific subcortical foci — non-specific, see clinical correlation.' Her mother had 'bad headaches with visual aura' throughout her reproductive years.
